narrative.text: Acknowledges the people behind the TB preventive treatment handbook, including its lead author and WHO Global TB Programme staff. It names the members, co-chairs and observers of the 2020 Guideline Development Group and the External Review Group. It also credits partners who supplied materials and notes that Unitaid funded design and layout.
A list of abbreviations and acronyms used in the TB preventive treatment handbook, covering regimens such as 3HP and 1HP, antiretroviral drugs, tests and programme terms.

Defines key terms used in the TB preventive treatment handbook, such as age groups, contact, household and close contact, index patient, high transmission setting and latent TB infection. Further definitions cover programmatic management, screening and treatment completion. It closes with a call to deliver preventive treatment to 30 million people by 2022 in line with the UN high-level meeting commitments.

Introduces the TB preventive treatment handbook, explaining that about a quarter of people worldwide are infected with M. tuberculosis and that people with HIV and contacts of TB patients are at highest risk. It places programmatic management of preventive treatment within the End TB Strategy and the 2018 UN high-level meeting targets, noting low coverage so far. It describes the handbook's purpose, intended users and approach of guiding countries through decision points. A box summarises WHO recommendations and urges governments and donors to expand access.

Discusses which at-risk populations countries should prioritise for systematic testing and TB preventive treatment, based on infection prevalence, progression risk and transmission. It sets out the rationale and WHO recommendations for people living with HIV, including children and infants, household contacts of all ages, and clinical risk groups such as patients on dialysis or anti-TNF therapy. It also covers prisoners, health workers, migrants and other groups that may be considered case by case. The chapter ends with implementation considerations for contact investigation and a call to invest in it.

Explains how to rule out TB disease before starting preventive treatment, since treating active disease this way risks delays and drug resistance. It reviews the sensitivity of symptom screening in different groups and the added value of chest radiography, citing related WHO recommendations. It discusses algorithms combining symptoms, imaging and tests for people with HIV, contacts and other risk groups. It ends with practical steps such as expanding rapid diagnostics, specimen transport and standard operating procedures.

Discusses the role of the tuberculin skin test and interferon-gamma release assays before preventive treatment, stressing there is no gold standard for TB infection. It explains how each test works, their limitations and false negatives, and when testing need not delay treatment, such as for people with HIV and young child contacts. It covers test choice, logistics and programme considerations, and includes an algorithm flowchart for deciding on preventive treatment. It ends with a call to invest in shorter regimens.

Covers the choice among WHO-recommended TB preventive treatment regimens, from six or nine months of isoniazid to shorter rifamycin-based options such as 3HP, 3HR, 1HP and 4R. It reviews evidence on efficacy and completion rates and explains the 2020 changes to recommended durations. It also addresses dosing, regimens for contacts of drug-resistant TB, pregnancy, children and drug interactions with antiretrovirals and other medicines. The chapter closes with guidance on people who use drugs and a call to raise demand for preventive treatment.

Addresses safety concerns that hinder scale-up of TB preventive treatment, including adverse drug reactions, monitoring and counselling. It tabulates known adverse events for isoniazid and rifamycins and details hepatotoxicity risks and their management. Further sections discuss interactions with other medicines, adherence, the durability of protection and fears that preventive treatment fosters drug resistance. It cites trial data finding no significant rise in rifampicin resistance and calls for patient support to ensure completion.

Chapter 7 of a WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) addresses how national programmes can help people complete their prescribed regimen. It explains that adherence depends on many personal, social and treatment-related factors and lists person-centred measures such as confidential counselling, education in the person's language, involving families and giving clear advice on side-effects. It also covers warning people that TB disease can still develop during TPT, along with options such as reminders, digital adherence technologies, shorter regimens and community support. The chapter closes by urging investment in monitoring and in digital tools for recording and reporting TPT services.

Chapter 8 of the TPT handbook sets out what data should be routinely recorded and reported, the minimum dataset for following people along the TPT cascade, and the tools for collecting it. It explains how monitoring and evaluation serve patient care, national programme management and global accountability, with examples such as counting household contacts evaluated and people completing TPT. Material on the cascade of care tracks numbers targeted, evaluated, eligible, started and completed, and explains how to estimate target populations among people living with HIV and household contacts. The chapter ends with a reminder that programmes must counsel people to make informed choices and protect them from stigma.

Chapter 9 of the TPT handbook discusses ethical considerations in delivering preventive treatment to people who are not ill or infectious. It stresses weighing individual benefits against harms, limiting testing and treatment to groups at proven risk, and ensuring that taking TPT is a voluntary, informed choice grounded in human rights. It also addresses equity, confidentiality, stigma and the need for adequate communication resources so that individuals and communities can decide autonomously.

Annex 1 of the TPT handbook lists key messages for ministries of health and for health care workers. Messages for ministries recall commitments made at the 2018 UN High-Level Meeting on TB and the End TB Strategy targets, and present TPT as an effective intervention that substantially lowers the risk of TB disease. Messages for health workers cover shorter rifapentine- or rifampicin-based regimens, which are reported to be easier to complete, plus counselling before treatment, ruling out TB disease and managing adverse events. Notes point to funding sources and to the Global Drug Facility for medicines.

Annex 2 recommends that ministries of health set up or strengthen a joint national coordinating body and a technical expert working group to drive scale-up of programmatic TPT management. It outlines their terms of reference, membership and secretariat arrangements, and asks TB and HIV programmes to fund regular meetings.

Annex 3 lists the main cost drivers to consider when budgeting for programmatic TPT management. These include target population sizes, tests for TB infection and chest radiography, human resources, medicines and procurement, and recording and reporting systems.

Annex 4 provides a planning checklist for programmatic TPT management, with columns for current status and next steps. Activities covered include strategic planning, guideline updates, coverage of risk groups, training, advocacy, community outreach and medicine supply and stock management.

Annex 5 answers frequently asked questions about the tuberculin skin test (TST) for TB infection. It explains how the test works, the standard tuberculin doses and intradermal injection technique, and how to read and measure the induration, including the ballpoint pen method. It also covers interpreting results, causes of false-positive and false-negative readings, and the limited effect of BCG vaccination given at birth.

Annex 6 answers frequently asked questions about interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) for TB infection, including the two commercial tests WHO reviewed in 2017. It explains that IGRAs measure interferon-gamma released by white blood cells exposed to M. tuberculosis-specific antigens absent from BCG strains, and that like TST they cannot separate infection from disease. It also covers specimen handling, interpretation and how to handle discordant or borderline results.

The reference list for the TPT handbook, citing studies on latent TB burden and prognosis, contact investigation and WHO strategies and guidelines, followed by the text of a patient information leaflet on TB infection and preventive treatment.

The front matter of the WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis preventive treatment (Module 1: Prevention), with title pages, ISBNs, the CC BY-NC-SA licence and disclaimers. It then gives the table of contents, running from the introduction through chapters on target populations, ruling out disease, testing, regimens and safety to annexes on planning and frequently asked questions about TST and IGRAs.
